claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is initially in a high-temperature BCC state.
Slow cooling at approximately 1 K/s permits limited atomic diffusion in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Aging at approximately 600°C permits sufficient diffusion for local chemical segregation and ordering without full equilibration.
The diffusion enabled by slow cooling and aging causes local segregation, especially of Al and correlated elements.
Local segregation leads to nucleation of nanoscale B2 or L12 ordered domains.
The nanoscale ordered domains form preferentially at grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Local ordered domains reduce the nucleation barrier for ordered-phase formation.
Formation of local ordered domains accounts for the range of phases observed after cooling.
Rapid quenching above 100 K/s suppresses diffusion-induced ordering.
Rapid quenching kinetically traps Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a predominantly metastable BCC state.
Rapidly quenched samples will contain negligible ordered precipitates.
Slow-cooled samples aged at 600°C will exhibit B2 or L12 ordered domains.
The volume fraction and definition of B2 or L12 domains will increase with aging time from 1 to 100 hours.
The mechanism should not manifest when the cooling rate is uniformly or extremely fast.
The proposed limited-ordering mechanism should not apply at excessively high aging temperatures because those conditions lead to full transformation.
Rapid-quenched and slow-cooled samples are to be compared after aging at 600°C for 1, 10, and 100 hours under an inert atmosphere.
TEM, XRD, EDS, and atom-probe tomography can be used to measure ordered-domain abundance, ordered-phase diffraction signatures, and chemical segregation.

Failure to observe a statistically significant increase in ordered-domain nucleation or volume fraction in slow-cooled and aged samples relative to rapidly quenched samples would falsify the hypothesis.
Observation of similar ordering in the rapid-quenched and slow-cooled conditions would falsify the proposed diffusion-kinetics explanation.

contradictions.description: The intervention wording can be read as applying the 600°C aging treatment only to the slow-cooled set, and the baseline is described as retaining minimal diffusion after quenching. The falsification design instead says both rapid-quenched and slow-cooled samples are aged for up to 100 hours, during which the quenched control may no longer represent a minimal-diffusion baseline.
